title: The Lucas/Kummer Digit Structure of Vanishing Hasse Derivatives of Xᵐ
description: The parent (factor-remainder-hasse-derivative-fq-oq-01) proved the overcounting dichotomy: over a characteristic-p field the ordinary iterated-derivative multiplicity test is exact when the true root multiplicity m < p and blind (every ordinary derivative vanishes at the root) once m ≥ p. Its first open question asks, in the unbounded regime m ≥ p, to STRATIFY by the base-p digits of m and describe how the ordinary test's blindness interacts with the Lucas/Kummer structure of the binomial coefficients C(m,k) that define hasseDeriv. This entry answers it for the pure power Xᵐ. First, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k)·X^(m-k) is a single monomial (hasseDeriv_X_pow), so over characteristic p it is nonzero exactly when C(m,k) survives reduction mod p: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ¬ p ∣ C(m,k) (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff). Feeding this into Mathlib's Lucas's theorem gives the full digit-domination criterion: writing m and k in base p, the k-th Hasse derivative survives iff every base-p digit of k is ≤ the corresponding digit of m (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits) — Kummer's carry-free condition. The blindness of the ordinary test is thus explained: it only ever reads the low orders k < p (scaled by the unit k!), yet the surviving orders are the digit-dominated k, which for m ≥ p spread all the way out to k = m. The count of surviving orders is ∏(dᵢ+1) over the base-p digits dᵢ of m (Glaisher/Fine), realized concretely over 𝔽₂: X³ (11₂) keeps all four orders k ≤ 3, while X⁴ (100₂) keeps only k ∈ {0,4}. 9 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries (decide, not native_decide).

mathlibDependencies.description: hasseDeriv k (monomial n r) = monomial (n-k) (↑(n.choose k) * r) — gives the closed form of the Hasse derivative of Xᵐ = monomial m 1 as the single monomial C(m,k)·X^(m-k).
Lucas's theorem: for p prime and m,k < p^a, C(m,k) ≡ ∏_{i<a} C(⌊m/pⁱ⌋ mod p)(⌊k/pⁱ⌋ mod p) [MOD p]. Turns the divisibility of C(m,k) into the base-p digit-domination condition.
p ∣ n! ↔ p ≤ n. Combined with C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! it shows a base-p digit a < p never introduces a factor of p into C(a,b) when b ≤ a.
For a prime p, p ∣ ∏ g i ↔ ∃ i, p ∣ g i. Reduces divisibility of the Lucas product to divisibility of a single digit binomial.
Over a ring of characteristic p, (n : R) = 0 ↔ p ∣ n. Converts vanishing of the monomial coefficient C(m,k) in the field into divisibility of the natural-number binomial.

originalContributions: hasseDeriv_X_pow: the closed form hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k)·X^(m-k) over any commutative ring, isolating the binomial coefficient C(m,k) as the single object controlling the k-th Hasse derivative of a pure power.

hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff / hasseDeriv_X_pow_eq_zero_iff: the bridge from polynomials to number theory — over a characteristic-p field, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) is (non)zero exactly when C(m,k) is (not) divisible by p, via monomial_eq_zero_iff and CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff.

not_dvd_choose_of_le_of_lt_prime and not_dvd_choose_digit_iff: the atomic single-digit Lucas fact — for a base-p digit a < p, C(a,b) avoids p exactly when b ≤ a — proved from C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! and p ∤ a! (a < p).

hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits: the capstone. Over a characteristic-p field, for m,k < p^a, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 iff every base-p digit of k is dominated by the corresponding digit of m — the Lucas/Kummer carry-free criterion, obtained by transferring divisibility across Mathlib's Lucas congruence and reducing the product to single digits. This directly answers the open question: the ordinary test reads only k < p (scaled by k!), but the surviving orders are the digit-dominated k, reaching k = m when m ≥ p.

nonzero_orders_X3_F2, nonzero_orders_X4_F2, hasseDeriv_X4_F2_profile: the digit count ∏(dᵢ+1) realized over 𝔽₂ — X³ (digits 11₂) keeps all four orders k ≤ 3 (count 2·2 = 4), while X⁴ (digits 100₂) keeps only k ∈ {0,4} (count 1·1·2 = 2), with the middle orders k = 1,2,3 vanishing.

relatedProblems.relationship: Parent: established the exact/unbounded overcounting dichotomy of the ordinary-derivative multiplicity test (exact for m < p, blind for m ≥ p) and asked, as its first open question, to stratify the unbounded regime by the base-p digits of m via the Lucas/Kummer structure of the hasseDeriv binomials. This entry answers that question for Xᵐ.

Grandparent: pins down the full failure profile of the ordinary multiplicity test in characteristic p (reliable to p−1, blind from p), the qualitative cutoff this entry refines to a digit-level criterion.

overview.historicalContext: Over a field of characteristic zero the multiplicity Factor Theorem certifies (X − a)^k ∣ f by the vanishing of f and its first k−1 ordinary derivatives. In characteristic p this collapses — derivative(X^p) = 0 — and Hasse's divided-power derivatives repair the criterion. The grandparent entry pins the collapse at a sharp cutoff (order p); the parent turns it into an all-or-nothing overcounting dichotomy for a general polynomial (exact for true multiplicity m < p, unbounded for m ≥ p). The natural refinement, and the parent's first open question, is arithmetic: in the unbounded regime the surviving Hasse derivatives are governed by the divisibility of binomial coefficients, whose mod-p behaviour is exactly Lucas's theorem (1878) and Kummer's carry count (1852).
overview.problemStatement: In the unbounded regime m ≥ p, stratify by the base-p digits of m: for the pure power Xᵐ over a field of characteristic p, determine exactly which Hasse derivatives hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) are nonzero, and express the answer through the Lucas/Kummer structure of the binomial coefficients C(m,k) that define hasseDeriv.
overview.proofStrategy: Reduce the polynomial question to a number-theoretic one, then apply Lucas. Step 1: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k)·X^(m-k) (hasseDeriv_X_pow, from hasseDeriv_monomial on Xᵐ = monomial m 1) is a single monomial, so over a field it vanishes iff its coefficient does — hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ¬ p ∣ C(m,k) (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff, via monomial_eq_zero_iff and CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff). Step 2: the single-digit fact — for a < p, ¬ p ∣ C(a,b) ↔ b ≤ a (not_dvd_choose_digit_iff): if b > a the binomial is 0 (divisible); if b ≤ a < p then C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! with p ∤ a! forces p ∤ C(a,b). Step 3: Mathlib's Lucas theorem writes C(m,k) ≡ ∏_{i<a} C(mᵢ,kᵢ) mod p (digits mᵢ = ⌊m/pⁱ⌋ mod p); divisibility transfers across the congruence (Nat.modEq_zero_iff_dvd) and a prime divides the product iff it divides some factor (Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff). Composing, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ∀ i < a, kᵢ ≤ mᵢ (hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits). The 𝔽₂ examples instantiate the count ∏(dᵢ+1).
keyInsights: For a pure power the Hasse derivative collapses to a single monomial hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k)·X^(m-k), so all the information about which orders survive is packed into the one binomial coefficient C(m,k).
Over characteristic p, survival of order k is purely arithmetic: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ p ∤ C(m,k). The polynomial question becomes a divisibility question about binomials.

Lucas's theorem converts that divisibility into a digit-domination condition: p ∤ C(m,k) iff every base-p digit of k is ≤ the corresponding digit of m — equivalently (Kummer) the addition k + (m−k) has no carries in base p.

This explains the parent's blindness precisely: the ordinary test can only read the low orders k < p (where k! is a unit), but the surviving Hasse orders are the digit-dominated k, which for m ≥ p extend all the way to k = m — far outside the ordinary test's window.

The number of surviving orders is ∏(dᵢ+1) over the base-p digits dᵢ of m (Glaisher/Fine). Over 𝔽₂ this is the count of odd binomials in row m of Pascal's triangle: X³ (11₂) keeps all 4 orders, X⁴ (100₂) keeps only 2.

sections.title: Closed Form and the Vanishing Criterion

sections.mathContext: Reduces the polynomial survival question for Xᵐ to the divisibility of a single binomial coefficient C(m,k) mod p.

sections.title: The Single-Digit Lucas Building Block
sections.summary: not_dvd_choose_of_le_of_lt_prime: for b ≤ a < p, p ∤ C(a,b), proved from C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! and p ∤ a!. not_dvd_choose_digit_iff: the biconditional ¬ p ∣ C(a,b) ↔ b ≤ a for a single base-p digit a < p (b > a gives C(a,b) = 0).
sections.mathContext: The atomic Lucas fact: within one base-p digit, a binomial coefficient avoids p exactly when the lower index is dominated by the upper.

sections.title: The Lucas Digit-Domination Criterion
sections.summary: hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits: for m,k < p^a over a characteristic-p field, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ∀ i < a, ⌊k/pⁱ⌋ mod p ≤ ⌊m/pⁱ⌋ mod p. Transfers divisibility of C(m,k) across Mathlib's Lucas congruence (Nat.modEq_zero_iff_dvd), reduces the product via Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff, and applies the single-digit criterion to each digit.
sections.mathContext: The complete answer to the open question: the surviving Hasse derivatives of Xᵐ are exactly the digit-dominated (carry-free) orders k.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 194 lines and 9 theorems answering the parent's first open question for the pure power Xᵐ. Over a field of characteristic p, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) is a single monomial C(m,k)·X^(m-k), so it is nonzero exactly when p ∤ C(m,k); Lucas's theorem then makes this a base-p digit-domination criterion — the k-th Hasse derivative survives iff every base-p digit of k is dominated by the corresponding digit of m (Kummer's carry-free condition). The count of surviving orders is ∏(dᵢ+1) over the base-p digits of m, realized concretely over 𝔽₂ by X³ (all four orders) and X⁴ (only k ∈ {0,4}).
conclusion.implications: This upgrades the parent's coarse regime split (m < p exact, m ≥ p blind) into a precise arithmetic description of the unbounded regime: even when the ordinary test sees nothing, the Hasse derivatives that survive are governed exactly by Lucas/Kummer. It pinpoints why the ordinary test fails — it inspects only the window k < p, whereas the surviving orders are the digit-dominated k, spread up to k = m — and it ties multiplicity detection in positive characteristic directly to the classical mod-p combinatorics of Pascal's triangle (Glaisher's odd-binomial count over 𝔽₂).
openQuestions: Extend the digit-domination criterion from the pure power Xᵐ to a general polynomial f: for a root a of true multiplicity m ≥ p, is the set of surviving Hasse-derivative orders still controlled by the base-p digits of m, or do the lower-order coefficients of f perturb it?

Make the count a theorem rather than a per-case computation: prove that the number of orders k with hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 over a characteristic-p field equals ∏(dᵢ+1) over the base-p digits dᵢ of m (the Glaisher/Fine formula), and identify the largest surviving order below p.
